newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU backs two-year transition in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: EU backs two-year transition in Bosnia.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers on Saturday endorsed a transition period in Bosnia that will keep the 15-nation bloc involved in the region for at least two more years.
"We want a two-year peace consolidation period," Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said after informal talks with his colleagues in the southern Irish town of Tralee.
Diplomats said international mediator Carl Bildt, who had earlier briefed the meeting, had also backed the idea.

They said that at this stage there was no agreement yet about what such a transition period would entail, but that it had been endorsed as a way of showing the various parties in Bosnia the EU planned to remain engaged long after elections on September 14.

The Irish EU presidency indicated that international involvement in Bosnia after 1996 would be needed for such areas as economic reconstruction, promotion of human rights, dealing with refugees, and ensuring regional stabilisation and arms control.
Bildt, the international community's high representative in Bosnia, said that preparations for the elections for regional and federal assemblies were progresssing well.
But he said rebuilding the country afterwards would be a still harder task.
"It is really now, after the elections, that we start to put the country together," he said, adding that the first task would be to agree a constitution for the divided country.
"That is going to be an extremely complex process," Bildt, the international community's high representative in Bosnia, told reporters.
Ireland also agreed to host a one-day conference on September 28 to win cash and manpower pledges for training a police force for post-war Bosnia.
Some 40 countries would be invited to the talks to get pledges of support for what Western states see as a cornerstone of Bosnia's recovery from civil war.
Commanders in NATO's Implementation Force IFOR say that the job of policing the streets and settling Moslem-Serb disputes should be in the hands of a civilian police force.
Irish diplomats said they expected the Dublin government, which is not a member of NATO, to pledge to help train the police but not to supply personnel.
Bildt said a lot of give and take would be needed in the country if it was to meet the goals of the Dayton peace agreement. "Everybody will have to lose something," he said, "but Bosnia will gain."
He reiterated his hope that the United States would remain in Bosnia with a military force after IFOR's mandate expired in December.
"It can be substantially smaller than IFOR," Bildt said of the force needed. "(But) it will have to have substantial military capabilities."
It was in America's interest. "They (the Americans) have invested a lot in Bosnia," he said.
He said negotiators were currently aiming at mid-November as the date to hold municipal elections. Elections at the local level, also due on September 14, were cancelled.
Bildt said that without local elected authorities it would be impossible for refugees to return home.
